vignette:
**The Weight of Footsteps**

Maya is a 48-year-old Vietnamese-American woman who has worked the floor of the same mid-sized restaurant for nearly a decade. She is known among her coworkers as dependable and warm — the one who remembers regulars' orders without writing them down, who stays late when someone calls in sick. To most people who see her moving efficiently between tables, she looks entirely in control. What they cannot see is the constant, low-grade surveillance she runs in her own mind, scanning every face that walks through the door.

It began three years ago, shortly after her divorce was finalized. A man she had briefly dated — a customer who had first come in alone on Tuesday evenings — began appearing in places he had no reason to be. Outside her apartment building. In the parking lot of her grocery store. Once, idling in a car across the street from her daughter's school. At first Maya told herself it was coincidence, the uncomfortable math of living in the same city. Then the notes started appearing under her windshield wipers. Then the calls from numbers she didn't recognize, silent on the other end. For fourteen months, he wove himself into the fabric of her ordinary life until nothing ordinary felt safe anymore.

The stalking ended — legally, at least — when a restraining order was issued after he followed her to a bus stop and grabbed her arm in broad daylight. He was charged, the contact stopped, and the legal system declared the matter resolved. Maya knows, rationally, that he has not contacted her in over a year. Her nervous system has not received that message.

She sleeps in fragments. Most nights she wakes between two and four in the morning, heart already pounding before she is fully conscious, certain she has heard something outside. She gets up and checks the locks — front door, back door, both windows in the bedroom — sometimes two or three times before she can lie back down. Even then, sleep rarely returns cleanly. She dreams of being followed through crowds where no one will look at her, of calling out and producing no sound.

At work, the hypervigilance takes on a particular texture. Every time the restaurant door opens, her body orients toward it before her mind does. Tuesday evenings are still the worst; she has asked to be taken off that shift and her manager, who knows nothing of the reason, has largely accommodated her. When a male customer lingers too long over his check, or when someone asks for her name, a cold clarity moves through her — not quite panic, but the immediate, total readiness of someone who has learned that danger can arrive in ordinary packaging. She has become skilled at excusing herself to the kitchen when the feeling gets too large to carry quietly.

She rarely talks about what happened. Her ex-husband knew some of it, but the marriage had already been fracturing, and she learned early that describing the fear out loud seemed to produce more skepticism than comfort. She has told her adult daughter only that she "went through something difficult." The isolation this creates is its own kind of weight. She describes herself as fine in a tone that closes the subject, and she has become so practiced at appearing capable that even people who care about her take her at her word.

What Maya carries most heavily is not the memory of any single incident but the permanent alteration of her relationship to the world. She used to enjoy walking home from the late shift, the city quiet and hers for a few minutes. Now she drives even the six blocks she used to walk without thinking. She used to trust her own read of people — it was part of what made her good at her job. Now she trusts the dread that rises in her chest faster than she trusts anything else. She is not sure which version of herself is more accurate, and she is not sure she will ever entirely know.
